https://www.southcoastregister.com.au/st.text: You may often book a holiday. But how often do you holiday a book? Sometimes it happens coincidentally. I recall one visit to the Moroccan city of Tangier, exploring the narrow alleys and stairs of its medina and being reminded of Paulo Coelho's The Alchemist. It's the first stop in the journey for the main character, Santiago, who finds work in a crystal shop after all his money is stolen, earning enough to make his way to Egypt. I encountered neither jewel nor heist but, like Santiago, it was another chapter in my journey. Sometimes it's a little more planned. Travelling in Spain, through the region of La Mancha, my itinerary is focused on the inspiration Miguel de Cervantes found for Don Quixote. His house is now a museum with lots to see, but it's up on nearby hills, at a series of 12 windmills, that you can really imagine how he and his delusional knight saw them as giants with thrashing arms. The idea of literary tourism is again front of mind with the release of The Odyssey. Even though the modern movie may be the spark for some "set-jetting", it's just taking a page from centuries of travel inspired by the ancient text, with Mediterranean itineraries through Turkiye, the Greek Islands, Sicily, and more. For years, people have used books to travel to novel destinations. While Pictures from Italy by Charles Dickens encouraged 19th-century tourists to embark on their own Grand Tour, modern readers journey to Canada's Prince Edward Island because of Anne of Green Gables or the Greek island of Corfu for Gerald Durrell's famous trilogy. Dracula inspires trips to Romania for the love of fantasy, while Eat Pray Love inspires trips to Bali for the fantasy of love. Perhaps even more common - and still a form of literary tourism - is reading a book set in a destination while you are setting foot there yourself. I've done it with Burmese Days in Myanmar, The Beach in Thailand, and In Patagonia... in Patagonia. Other popular holiday reads include My Brilliant Friend in Naples, Shantaram in India, and One Hundred Years of Solitude in Colombia (my Kindle broke when I was only halfway through... but I assume it's just another 50 years of solitude). Although James Joyce's Ulysses is a notoriously difficult read, there are ways to get a taste of the epic novel on a trip to Dublin without reading even one of its 265,000 words. A good place to start is one of the city's Martello Towers, which is where I found myself one trip. These stone cylindrical towers were built along the coast in the early 1800s as a defensive system against Napoleon, and eventually Joyce spent some time staying in one of them. He used that experience as the setting for the opening of Ulysses, and now the tower is a small museum that gives you another opening into the book. Of course, if you want to explore more chapters in person, head to Dublin on June 16 - the date on which the whole novel is set - for the annual Bloomsday festival. Although literary tourism has existed for centuries, it's now entering a new chapter. Bolstered by trends like slow travel, book clubs, and even viral online BookTok posts, more people than ever are turning over a new leaf in the way they travel for literature. It's now often about more than just visiting the destination - there's also been a boom in specialised reading tours. You can do a nine-day tour in the United States that sails along the Mississippi River, following the adventures of Huckleberry Finn and Mark Twain, including his family home and the limestone caves featured in Tom Sawyer. You can take a four-day tour in the Scottish Highlands to see the medieval sites in the Outlander books, or walk for six days through mountain passes and historic temples of Japan to explore trails captured by haiku master Matsuo Basho. Or go on a 20-day expedition in northern France to see the inspirations for a range of authors like Marcel Proust, Victor Hugo, and Gustave Flaubert. From Australia, ASA Cultural Tours offers 18 days in England's East Anglia browsing through the landscapes of Arthur Ransome, the marshes of Ruth Rendell, the retreats of Beatrix Potter, and many more. Meanwhile, a small company called Better Read Tours takes it a step further with a trip to Paris for two weeks to work on your own memoir, or a week in Stratford-upon-Avon in England for a creative writing workshop. READ MORE MICHAEL TURTLE: Even beyond writer retreats, we now also have reader retreats. The Literary Man Hotel in Portugal has 100,000 books to borrow during your stay. And some tour companies are taking people away... just so they can sit there and work through a book, like a four-day sailing trip around the Spanish island of Mallorca with an itinerary that reads, "leisurely breakfast on deck, sail south with stops for swims and reading time on deck". Or, closer to home, you can have two nights near Canberra with Reading Retreats Australia where you "let the outside world melt away for a weekend that's all about you and your books". It may seem odd to travel somewhere just to read, but if the aim of a holiday is to relax and experience a new world, then you can get both of those things from a good book. The best authors stay with you, so it's also no surprise you may want to find ways to connect to them in the real world. But ultimately, whether you're out in the landscapes or just in your hotel bed, there's a good holiday to be found between the covers.

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/29/izla.text: Menü Kereső Ki tudja, mi osztotta meg utoljára ennyire az izlandiakat Külföld A főváros, Reykjavík madártávlatból 2026. augusztus 12-én – Fotó: Denis Balibouse / File Photo / Reuters Molnár Zoltán Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Ha Északnyugat-Európa bármely országánál ezt látja az ember egy EU-ról szóló népszavazás előtt, valószínűleg megremeg a keze és előjön belőle az ijedség – már ha a mélyebb integráció híve: A felmérés jól mutatja, mekkora dilemmában vannak az izlandiak most, hogy arról szavazhatnak , szavazzanak-e majd egyszer újra az EU-csatlakozásról. A Maskína intézet augusztus 21–25. között készített közvélemény-kutatása borzasztó szoros eredményt jelzett előre. A támogatók 51,3 százalékkal vezetnek a 48,7 százalékra mért ellenzők előtt. A Reuters szerint a csatlakozáspártiak azért is aggódhatnak, mert egy előző, augusztus 13-i felmérésben még 52,2 százalékon álltak az igenek, tehát zárult az olló. A tét még úgy is óriási a 400 ezres szigetországnak, hogy a mostani népszavazás tehát nem arról szól , hogy Izland csatlakozzon-e az Unióhoz, hanem hogy egyáltalán folytassák-e a közel másfél évtizeddel ezelőtt megszakadt tárgyalásokat. Ha az igenek győznek, a tárgyalások újrakezdődnek, és ha minden csatlakozási feltételt sikerül kipipálni, akkor magáról a csatlakozásról is lenne egy újabb referendum, végül mind a 27 EU-tagállamnak rá kell bólintania a bővítésre. Az izlandi külügyminisztérium emlékeztetője szerint ha az igenek győznek szombaton, 2026 végén megkezdődhetnek a csatlakozási tárgyalások, amelyek ebben az esetben akár 18–24 hónap alatt le is pöröghetnek. Amikor ugyanis megszakadtak a tárgyalások, a 35 tárgyalási fejezetből már 11-et lezártak . Izland előző próbálkozása és helyzete A NATO-tag izlandi kormány hosszú éveken át ódzkodott az euroatlanti integráció másik pillérétől, az Európai Unióhoz és elődszervezeteihez történő csatlakozástól. A 2008-as pénzügyi világválság azonban az elsők között kényszerítette térdre az izlandi bankrendszert, és hirtelen népszerű lett a mentőmellényként is használható EU-tagság. Tárgyalások kezdődtek, azonban 2013-ban az akkori euroszkeptikus kormány befagyasztotta, majd 2015-ben teljesen leállította a közeledést. Az egyik érv az volt, hogy a szigetország így is tagja az európai közös piacnak, a schengeni övezetnek és az Európai Szabadkereskedelmi Társulásnak (EFTA), ahogy Norvégia, Svájc és Liechtenstein is. Viszont ezek az országok az uniós tagság hiányában nincsenek hatással a közös jogalkotásra, tehát nem befolyásolhatják azokat a szabályokat, amik aztán rájuk is vonatkoznak a közös piac vagy Schengen tekintetében. Ugyanakkor sok kis egyezség alapján Izland az uniós joganyag közel háromnegyedét már átültette a saját jogrendjébe, ezért is lenne lehetséges a hihetetlenül gyors csatlakozási procedúra. Csatlakozása esetén a 400 ezer fős Izland képviselőket küldhetne az Európai Parlamentbe, kormányfője és miniszterei helyet kapnának a Tanácsokban, fél évig lehetne az Európai Tanács soros elnöke, beléphetne a vámunióba és akár bevezethetné az eurót is. Vissza az asztalhoz? Miután a Kristrún Frostadóttir vezette balközép kormánykoalíció megnyerte a 2024-es, előrehozott parlamenti választást, ígéretet tett arra, hogy népszavazást tart a csatlakozási tárgyalások felmelegítéséről – írta a BBC . Ezt 2027-re tervezték, de a geopolitikai folyamatok miatt előrehozták egy évvel. A Reuters szerint az újabb EU-s próbálkozás mögött olyan faktorok állnak, mint az elszállt megélhetési költségek és az ukrajnai háború. Miután Donald Trump amerikai elnök folyton a szomszédos – a dán korona alá tartozó – Grönland elfoglalásával fenyegetőzött , az izlandiak még inkább Európa felé kezdtek húzni. A helyzetnek nem tett jót az új amerikai nagykövet viccelődése sem arról, hogy Izland lesz az USA 52. tagállama, ahogy az sem, hogy Trump davosi beszédében többször is Izlanddal keverte össze Grönlandot. A Politico több izlandi politikust is megszólaltatott a kampányról. Egy név nélkül nyilatkozó szociáldemokrata képviselő arról beszélt, hogy Grönland ügye nincs rendezve, Trump pedig „eléggé szókimondó volt, nemcsak tavaly, hanem újra meg újra”. Szerinte az utca embere sokat gondol erre. Dagur Eggertsson volt reykjavíki polgármester, egyben Izland delegációvezetője a NATO Parlamenti Közgyűlésében egyetértett Mark Carney kanadai miniszterelnökkel abban, hogy „a kis- és középhatalmaknak össze kell fogniuk”, ami sürgetőbb, mint valaha. A megkérdezett helyiek azt mondták, tartanak Oroszországtól, de már az Egyesült Államokat sem tartják megbízható szövetségesnek. „Egy olyan nyitott gazdaság, mint Izland esetén a fokozott nemzetközi együttműködésnek van értelme, de nyilván mindannyiunknak vannak fenntartásaink” – mondta egy korábbi interjúban Frostadóttir miniszterelnök a Bloomberg szerint. Hozzátette, Izland szigetország, az emberek életvitele sokban különbözik attól, amilyen a kontinensen élőké. Egy férfi egy kampányplakát előtt pózol Reykjavíkban – Fotó: Leonhard Foeger / Reuters Eiríkur Bergmann, a Bifröst Egyetem professzora szerint a szuverenitás az izlandi politika magva, amióta 1944-ben függetlenedtek Dániától. Mindkét tábor a szuverenitásra hivatkozik a kampányban: a csatlakozáspártiak szerint ezt kiterjesztené az EU-tagság, az ellenzők szerint éppen hogy fenyegetné. Az Előre Izland nevű nempárti tábor és a Függetlenségi Párt vezetője, Guðlaugur Þór Þórðarson azt mondta a Politicónak, Izland jelenlegi európai integrációja elegendő, nincs szükség EU-csatlakozásra. A korábbi külügyminiszter szerint is felháborítók Trump szavai Grönlandról, de szerinte az amerikai kormányok jönnek és mennek, a fontos az Izland és az USA közti kétoldalú védelmi egyezmény és a NATO-tagság, főképp, hogy Izlandnak nincs saját hadserege. Eggertsson ugyanakkor azt mondta, a sarkvidék már nem olyan nyugalmas hely, a klímaváltozás miatt olvad a jég, új hajózási útvonalak nyílnak meg. Talán ennek is betudható , hogy Izland az EU-val is védelmi megállapodást kötött márciusban. Jelen van a város–vidék ellentét is a kérdésben. Reykjavík és agglomerációja jobban igenpárti, vidéken viszont a nemek dominálnak. A tízezres Selfoss felé autózva szénabálákon van jelen a nemkampány szlogenje – vette észre a Politico. Van, aki azt mondja, a nemmel szavazó gazdákra és halászokra hallgat, de volt, aki a magas béreket felzabáló, száguldó (5,6 százalék) infláció és a volatilis izlandi koronánál (króna) stabilabb euró miatt örülne a tagságnak. Van olyan is, aki a BBC-nek azt mondta, ha most nemmel szavaz, nem tudja meg, mit is kínálna országának az EU, és a mostani szavazás még úgysem a tagságról dönt. A csatlakozás a hal(rém)álom Külön ki kell térni az izlandi halászatra, ami a helyi gazdaság gerince, tavaly az export kétötödét adta a BBC adatai szerint. A nemek tábora szerint az EU beleavatkozna az izlandi szuverenitásba, főleg a politikailag kényes halászati és agrárügyekben. A legutóbbi izlandi tárgyalások is a halászati kvótákon bicsaklottak meg. A félelem erős, hogy az EU közös halászati politikája halban gazdag vizekre engedné be a többi tagország halászhajóit. Még az igenek táborában is megkérdőjelezhetetlen, hogy ebben nem engedhetnek. A kormány azt tervezi, hogy a tárgyalásokon egyfajta halászati opt-outot, kivételezést harcol ki magának, ha már korábban a finnek és a svédek is kialkudtak mezőgazdasági kivételeket. „Egy tagállamnak sem garantáltak állandó opt-outot” – mondta a BBC-nek Margrét Ágústa Sigurðardóttir, az Izlandi Gazdaszövetség vezetője. Ő attól fél, hogy az EU több szakpolitikája inkább a 450 millió fogyasztó érdekeit nézi, semmint a 400 ezer izlandiéit. A 16 éves kora óta halászó, a britekkel a halászati területi szembenállást – a tőkehalháborút – is végigcsináló Sigurdur Thórdarson azt mondta a Telegraphnak : „Ha csatlakoznánk az Európai Unióhoz, az izlandiakat túlszabályoznák. Ez borzalmas lenne a halászoknak.” A lap által megszólaltatott Hjörtur J. Gudmundsson, az EU–izlandi kapcsolatok szakértője árnyalta a képet: szerinte itt nem pusztán a halról van szó, hanem „a hal inkább jelképe a szuverenitásunknak”. Szerinte a csatlakozás lenullázná a part menti halászfalvakat, ahogy ezt ő EU-szerte látta már. Mások attól félnek, a csatlakozás után a nagy halászati cégek felvásárolnák a kisebb izlandiakat és flottáikat. EU-ellenes tüntetők Reykjavíkban, 2026. augusztus 27-én – Fotó: Leonhard Foeger / Reuters Kristján Loftsson, Izland utolsó bálnavadásza se lelkes, még pénzt is adott a nemkampánynak. Az Unió ugyanis tiltja a bálnavadászatból származó termékek kereskedelmét. Loftsson ezért is nevezte a szabályozás iránt megszállott, szocialista, kommunista berendezkedésű blokknak az Európai Uniót. Brüsszel lelkes, Oslo les Az biztos, hogy Brüsszelben nagy öröm lenne, ha Izland csatlakozna, ugyanis nagyon rég volt nyugati irányú bővítés az EU-ban – sőt inkább veszteség volt a brexittel és Nagy-Britannia távozásával. Egy nempárti győzelem szombaton ezért fájdalmas csapás lenne az EU vezetőinek. A Bloomberg szerint a nyugat-balkáni országok , Moldova és Ukrajna csatlakozási folyamata mellett Izlanddal is egy pozitív jelzést akar küldeni az EU. Ehhez akár engedményekre is hajlandó. „Izland döntése vitán felül megerősítené az EU ügyét, hogy új tagokat üdvözöljön” – mondta a Bloombergnek Marta Kos bővítési biztos. Külön érdekes, milyen hullámokat vetne Skandináviában az izlandi igenek győzelme. A svédek, finnek, dánok és a közeli balti országok is EU-tagok, Norvégia az egyedüli kivétel. Itt már két népszavazást is tartottak a múltban a tagságról, 1974-ben 53,5–46,5 százalékos arányban, 1994-ben 52,2–47,8 százalékos arányban győztek a nemek. Espen Barth Eide norvég külügyminiszter az Euronews szerint már elismerte, az izlandi csatlakozási folyamat miatt különleges helyzetbe kerülne országa, szinte magára maradna az EFTA-ban. A norvég ABC Nyheter lap felmérése szerint jelenleg 49 százalék ellenzi és 37 támogatja a csatlakozást. A norvégok fő baja szintén a halászat, agrárium és kereskedelem, de a napokban az olajfúrások miatt is szembekerültek az Unióval. (Chris Sweda/Chicago Tribune) By Rev Larry Pickens PUBLISHED: September 27, 2026 at 8:00 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Exodus 16:2-3: “The whole congregation of the Israelites complained against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness. The Israelites said to them, ‘If only we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate our fill of bread, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger.’” On Christmas morning 1966, our Chicago block erupted when apparently all of the kids received Walkie Talkies as presents. We prepared our devices, ran outside and began talking all over the neighborhood. It sounded akin to a party line. During the cacophony of our radio calls, a policeman whose car routinely sat at the curb outside my house to catch people running the stop sign in the nearby intersection got on our transmissions to say, “Would you fools stop talking on those Walkie Talkies.” Apparently, we were jamming the police officer’s ability to receive his police calls. At the age of 10 years old I received my first lesson in community organizing. James Brown once did a song that was played every Christmas; it was titled “Santa Claus Goes Straight to the Ghetto.” The song was a rallying point for people like me to feel good about our beings and place in the world. I grew up in Chicago’s Englewood community, where I felt accepted and understood my worth. However, there were other dynamics present that I did not understand as a child. My segregated community was systemically created and designed economically, politically and socially to keep me and my people confined to that small space in our Black world. I really did not understand the existential ramifications of my “ghetto” until I visited the Jewish Ghetto in Warsaw, Poland, where the Nazis built a wall around the Jewish community with the intention of exterminating them. The Jews fought back, they stood up to evil, and they died like women, like men, like human beings. I have been to Gaza and the West Bank; both have walls around them, built by Israel. In 2026 Israel and Israeli settlers are systematically (economically, socially, politically, violently and militarily) choking Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza — in ghettos. Should Palestinians resist? I think so. I want to suggest that the Scripture text represents vulnerability and uncertainty, which created within the traumatized community a slave mentality. In the wilderness, instead of thanking Moses and Aaron for their liberation and the opportunity to move forward, the people focused on the cost of liberation and hearkened back to their enslavement because their oppression felt more comfortable and predictable. We shun the unknown journey attached to our liberation because we are afraid of the uncertainty it brings. We are frozen in our enslavement because of the cost of freedom; we find it to be too great. Franz Fanon, in his book “Black Faces, White Masks,” described the psychological impact of colonialism that forced many African people to hate their own Black skin and culture while seeking to emulate their oppressors, viewing European white skin and culture as being superior to their own. Israel had also decided enslavement was superior to their own liberation struggle. Our bodies are not free until our minds are free. Another story about my neighborhood: I can remember that the high school was next to our grammar school. At lunch break when we could go outside on the campus, it was not unusual to see some high school students sniffing airplane glue from plastic bags. We were of course impressionable children, but I read a lot and was privileged to understand the neurological effects glue sniffing would have on my brain. It would have been easy to succumb to that world of addiction but knowledge — self-knowledge — gave me a way out. Freedom is tied to knowing the boundaries and horizons of our possibilities. Only God has the capacity to define your worth. Too often we allow ourselves to be defined by the narratives and expectations that others try to place upon us. I find Toni Morrison’s phrase “emotional laziness” so useful because it is so easy for us to acquiesce, succumb to the limitations placed upon us by our environments, our communities, even our “friends and loved ones.” Others cannot define our reality when God has given each one of us the ability to do that for ourselves. Enslavement can be an abusive relationship, systemic bondage, addiction, a mindset, anything that locks us into complacency and victimhood. Some of us are amazingly comfortable in our bondage. Theologian Richard Rohr, in “Simplicity: The Freedom of Letting Go,” uses scriptural imagery — like the man in the tombs bound by chains — to point out that human beings often feel more comfortable and familiar with their psychological or spiritual “slavery” than with the radical demands of actual freedom. True freedom, Rohr says, requires assuming radical responsibility for ourselves, whereas being spiritually enslaved means constantly having someone or something else to blame for our condition. No one but God can determine your worth and your capacity. We are not called to align ourselves with empire, colonialism, or power; our call is to fulfill the Gospel of Jesus Christ centered in the recognition and respect of the divine image in every human being. The Imago Dei. One of my favorite musicals is Les Misérables. It is of course a depiction of the French Revolution. One of the songs, “Do You Hear the People Sing,” speaks of revolution in a poignant way: Do you hear the people sing? Singing the song of angry men? It is the music of the people Who will not be slaves again! When the beating of your heart Echoes the beating of the drums There is a life about to start When tomorrow comes! Will you join in our crusade? Who will be strong and stand with me? Beyond the barricade Is there a world you long to see? Then join in the fight That will give you the right to be free! This is a contributed opinion column. The Rev. Larry Pickens is the executive director of the Pennsylvania Council of Churches. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c920.text: Image source, Getty Images By Bernd Debusmann Jr Â and Â Mike Hills Published 26 October 2026, 11:29 GMT Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message. When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since. Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts. But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress. Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency. He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both. But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far. His signature policy has played out in five key ways. 1. A border that is largely closed Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border. His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing. When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted. By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone. On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings. To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach. That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north. "President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October. "The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works." 2. Building of wall speeding up A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign. Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (Â£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill. According to government figures , external , about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US. Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction. Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated. Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate. "Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council. There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging. Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it. "I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history." Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning Published 3 days ago 3. Detentions and deportations rocketing Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country. During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first. Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project , external , a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA. But the same data , external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%. Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office. But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead. A New York Times and Siena poll , external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength. A separate poll, from Politico and Public First , external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive. Figure caption, Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms 4. Refugee intake down sharply After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests. In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied. The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation". Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African. By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela. Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to. One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US. Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again Published 5 days ago 5. A squeeze on visas - and a $1m golden ticket Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes. Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel. Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down. And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers , mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X , external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%. "The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added. While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive. One study, from the Wharton School of Business , external , found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth. Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million. The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee. At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.
